transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-07 16:00 UTC; Duration: ~75m; Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SA), Maya Patel (Aurelia Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Infra Lead), Liam O'Connor (CTO), Sara Novak (Security), Ethan Brooks (SRE).

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'll hand to priya for the agenda.
[00:22] Priya Raman: hi all, thanks. Today we want to focus on autoscaling and capacity planning — reserved GPUs, burst policies, queueing models, and some practical tips for KV cache warmup and batching tradeoffs. we'll cover POC steps near the end.
[01:05] Maya Patel: sounds good. Our primary constraint is predictable latency for clinical scoring, we can't have big tail spikes. We also have strict data residency and need the private deployment option.
[01:27] Carlos Ruiz: yeah and our infra team is worried about cost — reserved capacity vs bursts — how to size for peak without overpaying.
[01:40] Priya Raman: totally. first, quick baseline questions — what's your target p50/p95 and typical request size?
[01:55] Maya Patel: p50 we'd like < 80 ms generating short summaries (under 256 tokens). p95 we want under 350 ms, 99th under 600 absolute maximum. traffic pattern is spiky — daily scheduled spikes at 09:00 and 17:00 with bursts up to 120 rps for about 5-7 minutes, otherwise 6-12 rps baseline.
[02:20] Ethan Brooks: we also sometimes run batch retrospective scoring overnight where throughput matters more than latency.
[02:30] Jordan Lee: ok good. so two profiles: real-time low-latency interactive, and throughput-oriented batch. For low-latency we recommend pinned dedicated instances with small burst buffers. For batch, autoscaled shared pools are fine.
[02:52] Liam O'Connor: when you say burst buffers, is that a fixed standby GPU or a queueing mechanism?
[03:02] Priya Raman: both. Redwood Dedicated supports reserved replicas (pinned GPUs) for baseline capacity plus a burst policy where short bursts route to a cheaper shared pool or extra reserved on-demand nodes. the burst is policy-driven — you can set burst duration, max concurrent burst replicas, and fallback model variants.
[03:30] Carlos Ruiz: how do you model queueing? if we let requests queue, tail latency explodes. we'd rather reject or degrade.
[03:42] Priya Raman: we use a Q-model approximation internally — requests are either served immediately if there's capacity, enqueued in a short in-memory request queue (a few hundred ms by default) and then scheduled into batching windows. long queueing is avoided by our admission controller which can reject or reroute to a faster model variant. In practice we tune queue depth, batch timeout, and max batch size to hit the p95 target.
[04:10] Maya Patel: can you explain KV cache warmup? our use case has many unique prefixes so cache hit rates might be low.
[04:22] Priya Raman: sure. KV cache (sometimes transcribed in our notes as K V cash) stores key-value activations for autoregressive decoding. For interactive sessions with repeated prefixes, you get big savings. For many unique prefixes we recommend prefill strategies — for example, prefetch common system prompts and medical templates during low traffic, or use a small prewarm pool that keeps KV for the most common routes. Additionally, we recommend tuning response chunk sizes so that early partial responses don't force recomputation.
[05:00] Carlos Ruiz: is prefill done at request time or as a background job?
[05:06] Priya Raman: background prefill jobs are common — we can script prefill from a shared bucket of top prompts. On Dedicated you can also persist warm KV across short model restarts if you use sticky routing.
[05:25] Alex Chen: a quick note on quantization — moving to 4-bit quantization boosted throughput in our tests but increased variability in tail latency on some models. Priya, do you want to add details?
[05:40] Priya Raman: yeah. quantization reduces memory/GPU utilization so you get more concurrent contexts per GPU and higher RPS. downside is decoding can be noisier and GPU kernel dispatch patterns change — sometimes you see a higher p99 because small matrix ops are less optimized. we recommend lab testing on the exact model + sequence lengths. for clinical, quality is also a validator so run eval sets in the loop.
[06:14] Maya Patel: do you support mixed-mode — quantized for batch, FP16 for live?
[06:21] Priya Raman: yes, routing by profile is supported — live low-latency routes to FP16 pinned capacity, nightly batch to quantized nodes. autoscaler policy can prefer one pool over another.
[06:36] Ethan Brooks: on the topic of autoscaler, is it reactive or predictive?
[06:43] Jordan Lee: it's hybrid — you can use predictive rules based on traffic schedules plus reactive scale-up. predictive rules are important for known daily spikes. reactive scale-up is fast (seconds for warm shared nodes, but minutes for cold-started reserved GPUs). so we recommend a small cushion of reserved GPUs to absorb the first 30-90s of spikes while we bring more capacity.
[07:10] Carlos Ruiz: what's a recommended cushion for our 5-7 minute bursts at 120 rps?
[07:16] Priya Raman: rough calc — if baseline is 8 rps and peak 120 rps, you need headroom ~15x. we usually size reserved GPUs to handle baseline + 20-40% of expected burst, and let the burst pool cover the rest. for you that might be 1-2 pinned A10s for baseline and 2-3 burst-capable GPUs depending on model size and prompt length. we'll validate in the POC.
[07:43] Maya Patel: can you run the numbers? our model is a 7B variant, avg 150 tokens per request.
[07:50] Priya Raman: yes, we'll add the estimated tokens/sec per GPU and give a sizing table — that's part of the benchmark sheet.
[07:58] Liam O'Connor: curious about backpressure and client retries — do you provide retry semantics or 429 responses?
[08:06] Priya Raman: we support configurable admission control. for live low-latency routes we often return 429 when queues exceed threshold and route to a degraded classification model or cached result. for non-critical requests we accept queuing with a max wait. You can also configure client-side exponential backoff.
[08:27] Sara Novak: security question — if we use Dedicated or Private, how does VPC peering and subnet mapping work? We need SAML SSO + SOC2 audit logs.
[08:38] Alex Chen: Dedicated offers VPC peering and private link options; Private (on-prem/VPC) gives you customer-managed control plane. We have KMS integrations for key management and audit logs that meet SOC 2 requirements. We'll share the security pack.
[08:55] Sara Novak: please include retention windows for audit logs and options to push to our SIEM.
[09:02] Alex Chen: noted.
[09:08] Priya Raman: back to autoscaling — another lever is batching. increasing max batch size increases GPU utilization but adds batching latency. We typically tune the batch timeout (for example 5-20 ms) and max batch size. For p50-sensitive endpoints we set a small timeout and smaller batch sizes; for batch endpoints we increase both.
[09:35] Ethan Brooks: do you do continuous batching across requests from different customers? any concerns about tenant isolation?
[09:42] Priya Raman: batch mixing is supported but we keep tenant isolation guarantees — no cross-tenant data leakage in the model; batching only groups compute kernels. There are knobs to disable cross-tenant batching for extra isolation if needed.
[09:58] Maya Patel: earlier you mentioned model variants as fallback. can you give an example?
[10:05] Priya Raman: yes — if the primary 7B FP16 model is saturated, you can fallback to a smaller tuned 3B quantized variant with a lower cost and lower latency for certain queries, or to a retrieval-augmented pipeline that returns a lightweight structured answer. It's policy-driven per route.
[10:28] Carlos Ruiz: how do you handle warm KV across model variant fallback? we don't want to lose context.
[10:36] Priya Raman: good point — KV isn't compatible across model architectures. for fallbacks we either fall back to models that share tokenizers/architectures or we use a stateless degrade where we summarize the prefix and re-encode. There's a tradeoff in fidelity.
[10:55] Alex Chen: quick interruption — can we share a short perf story? last quarter we did a customer benchmark where adding a 30% reserved cushion cut p95 by half on daily spikes.
[11:05] Maya Patel: that's compelling. can you quantify cost delta?
[11:10] Alex Chen: yes, Priya will include cost estimates per GPU-hour for the reserved vs burst mix.
[11:18] Priya Raman: note that Dedicated committed pricing can change the math — reserved monthly commitments lower per-hour costs; bursts to shared pools are pay-as-you-go. We'll show a blended TCO example in the spreadsheet.
[11:32] Ethan Brooks: about POC telemetry — what logs do you need from us?
[11:38] Jordan Lee: we'll need sample traces (headers, prompt lengths, token counts), and network topology for VPC peering. We'll also ask for a small synthetic load generator to reproduce traffic patterns.
[11:52] Maya Patel: we'll provide anonymized traces and a traffic schedule.
[11:58] Carlos Ruiz: network egress and peering — is there any special firewall rule we need to open?
[12:05] Alex Chen: outbound peering on standard ports, and we use mutual TLS for control plane. We'll share a checklist.
[12:15] Priya Raman: for the POC we recommend running three phases: baseline characterization (1-2 days), stress tests including burst scenarios (2-3 days), and a validation run for the tuned config (2 days). total ~1 week.
[12:35] Maya Patel: timeline — we can start week of 2026-04-20 if we get the checklist and perf sheet soon.
[12:43] Priya Raman: perfect. we'll also propose initial autoscaler policies: reserved handles baseline + 30% burst cushion; reactive autoscale for up to X nodes with warm-up timers; short admission queue capped at 200 ms; fallback to 3B quantized variant after 500 ms wait.
[13:10] Liam O'Connor: what's the warm-up time for cold-managed GPUs?
[13:15] Priya Raman: cold start for a model load is typically 2-7 minutes depending on model size and infra. warm shared nodes that have cached kernels are faster (tens of seconds). That's why predictive scheduling or reserved cushions matter.
[13:32] Ethan Brooks: do you persist model weights on disk across restarts or pre-load into staging?
[13:38] Jordan Lee: weights are in an object store and we stream to GPUs; for Dedicated we can pre-stage weights on local SSDs to reduce cold-start. We'll document pros/cons.
[13:50] Carlos Ruiz: what about telemetry for queue depth and batch sizes? we need dashboarding hooks.
[13:56] Priya Raman: Redwood Console provides per-route metrics for queue depth, batch size histogram, per-token latency, KV hit rate, and GPU utilization. We can give dashboard templates.
[14:08] Maya Patel: can we get an alert if KV hit rate drops below a threshold?
[14:12] Priya Raman: yes, alerts for KV hit-rate, p95 latency, and CPU/GPU saturation are configurable.
[14:22] Alex Chen: quick note — when we ran the numbers with a 7B at 150 tokens avg, typical tokens/sec per A10-ish GPU was X in our internal tests; we'll include a table with exact numbers per model and per sequence length in the benchmark sheet.
[14:40] Maya Patel: again, some transcriptions in our notes might spell Redwood features oddly — just want to confirm: Dedicated = reserved capacity; Private = customer-managed?
[14:49] Alex Chen: correct. Dedicated is SLA-backed reserved pools; Private is customer-pinned control plane, can be VPC or on-prem.
[15:00] Priya Raman: ok, any other questions on queueing or batching?
[15:06] Ethan Brooks: curious about multi-stage pipelines — we call a classifier then generator. how to size end-to-end?
[15:15] Priya Raman: size for the slowest stage but you can decouple stages: run classifier on smaller quantized nodes, generator on FP16 reserved nodes. Then autoscale each stage independently and use async queues between them.
[15:32] Carlos Ruiz: retries across stages — if generator fails should classifier keep state? we want idempotency.
[15:40] Jordan Lee: modelled with idempotent request IDs and replay logs; we can recommend patterns.
[15:49] Maya Patel: OK. can you include advice on token-limited prompts? we saw costs blow up when prompts had full patient histories.
[15:58] Priya Raman: yes, recommend prompt engineering: summarize prior context, use retrieval to supply condensed context, and set max input token cutoff. We'll include examples.
[16:12] Alex Chen: let's recap next steps. Priya will share perf sheet & perf traces; Alex will send pricing + security appendix; Aurelia to provision VPC peering and provide anonymized traces; schedule POC week of 2026-04-20. Any objections?
[16:28] Maya Patel: all good.
[16:32] Sara Novak: please include SOC2 evidence and audit retention options.
[16:36] Alex Chen: will do.
[16:40] Ethan Brooks: quick final Q on rollback/fallback during incidents — do you have automated rollbacks if a rollout increases latency?
[16:47] Priya Raman: yes, we support automatic rollback policies (canary thresholds on p95 and error rate) and sticky routing back to previous model revision.
[16:55] Liam O'Connor: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[17:00] Alex Chen: thanks all — action owners and dates captured. We'll follow up with docs and links.

Notes: occasional transcript errors present (speaker overlaps, mis-typed product names). References shared during the call: link: benchmark_sheet.xlsx (shared by Redwood), link: security_pack.pdf (shared by Alex).

End of transcript.
